stem_md: For a positive integer  $n\geq 3$  plot  $n$  equally spaced points around a circle.  Label one of them  $A$ , and place a marker at  $A$ .  One may move the marker forward in a clockwise direction to either the next point or the point after that.  Hence there are a total of  $2n$  distinct moves available; two from each point.  Let  $a_n$  count the number of ways to advance around the circle exactly twice, beginning and ending at  $A$ , without repeating a move.  Prove that  $a_{n-1}+a_n=2^n$  for all  $n\geq 4$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let us label each point with  $1$  or  $2$  and for every point you move the labeled number of points forward if it is the first time the point is visited and the other move if it is the second time the point is visited.  Call a labeling " $n$ -good" if it results in advancing around the circle exactly twice beginning and ending at  $A$  and call it " $n$ -bad" otherwise.  Note that in an  $n$ -bad labeling, the point before  $A$  must be visited the second time around and it must move forward two points when visited the second time around (since it must skip  $A$  the second time around).

I will show that there exists a bijection between  $n$ -bad labelings and  $n-1$ -good labelings.

First let us take an  $n$ -bad labeling and remove the point right before  $A$ .  There are two cases, the point we removed was labeled  $1$  and the point we removed was labeled  $2$ .

<details><summary>**<u>Case 1:</u>***The point we removed was labeled 1*</summary>Then the point we removed must have been visited the first time around as well as the second time around (at which it moves forward two points).  Note that since said point is visited the first time around and it is labeled  $1$ ,  $A$  must also be visited the first time around.  Then after removing said point, the same path will be traveled up until the point we removed and instead of the marker being moved to the point we removed, it will be moved to  $A$ .  Then the same path will be traveled for the second time around and instead of visiting the point we removed the second time around, it will once again visit  $A$  and therefore is a  $n-1$ -good labeling.</details>

<details><summary>**<u>Case 2:</u>***The point we removed was labeled 2*</summary>Then the point we removed must have not been visited the first time around and must be visited the second time around.  Obviously two points in a row cannot both be skipped when going around once since the maximum number of points that can be skipped consecutively is one.  Therefore, since the point we removed was skipped once the first time around, the point before the point we removed must have been labeled a  $2$  in order to skip said point the first time around.  Thus after removing said point, the marker's path will be the same up until the point we removed at which it will visit the point right before the point we removed and skip  $A$ .  Then at the second time around, it obviously must visit either  $A$  or the point right before the point we removed.  If it visits  $A$  then the new labeling is an  $n-1$ -good labeling.  If it visits the point right before the point we removed, then it must move forward one point (since it already moved forward two points from that point) and thus the marker will be moved to  $A$  - making the new labeling an  $n-1$ -good labeling.</details>

Thus, we have showed that deleting a point in an  $n$ -bad labeling results in a unique  $n-1$ -good labeling and therefore our mapping is injective.

Now we will show that our mapping is also surjective.

Take a  $n-1$ -good labeling and add a point right before  $A$ .  Then there are two cases, the point right before  $A$  in the  $n-1$ -good labeling was labeled  $1$  and the point right before  $A$  in the  $n-1$ -good labeling was labeled  $2$ .

Note that in any path around the circle twice, each point must be visited at least once.  Assume the contrary, then a point  $P$  must be skipped twice.  The only possible way that can happen is if the marker visits the point right before  $P$  twice and moves two points forward on both occasions, which violates the condition that no moves can be repeated.  Thus, each point must be visited at least once.

<details><summary>**<u>Case 1:</u>***The point right before  $A$  was labeled 1*</summary>In this case, we will insert a point right before  $A$  that is also labeled  $1$ .
<details><summary>**<u>Case 1a:</u>***The point two points before  $A$  was labeled 1*</summary>In this case, the point right before  $A$  must have been visited the second time around because either the point right before  $A$  or the point two points before  $A$  must be visited the second time around and if the point two points before  $A$  is visited the second time around, the marker will move one point forward and visit the point right before  $A$  the second time around.  Thus in both cases the point right before  $A$  will be visited the second time around.  However, since the point right before  $A$  will not be visited the first time around, the point two points before  $A$  will be visited the first time around and since it is labeled  $1$ , the marker will visit the point right before  $A$  the first time around, which is a contradiction.  Thus this case is not possible.</details>
<details><summary>**<u>Case 1b:</u>***The point two points before  $A$  was labeled 2*</summary>In this case, in the  $n-1$ -good labeling,  $A$  must have been visited the first time around because either the point before  $A$  (labeled 1) or the point two points before  $A$  (labeled 2) must be visited the first time around which both result in moves of the marker to  $A$ .  Then after inserting the new point labeled  $1$ , the path of the marker will be the same as the path it takes in the  $n-1$ -good labeling except the marker will visit the newly inserted point instead of  $A$  when it reaches it (since in the  $n-1$ -good labeling it reaches  $A$ ) but then it will once again move to  $A$  since the newly inserted point is labeled  $1$ .  Then the path will continue to be identical since in the  $n-1$ -good labeling, the marker visits  $A$  the first time around and then the second time around it will again visit the newly inserted point right before  $A$ .  However, the only available move is two moves forward so it will skip  $A$  and therefore the new labeling is an  $n$ -bad labeling.</details></details>

<details><summary>**<u>Case 2:</u>***The point right before  $A$  was labeled 2*</summary>In this case, we will insert a point right before  $A$  that is also labeled  $2$ .  Thus, since the point right before  $A$  in the  $n-1$ -good labeling must be visited at least once, it must have been visited the first time around (because if it was visited the second time around, it would have skipped  $A$  and therefore would not be an  $n-1$ -good labeling).  Thus, after inserting the new point, the marker will travel the same path as in the  $n-1$ -good labeling until the point that was right before  $A$  at which it will skip the point we inserted and move to  $A$ .  Then at the second time around, it must visit either the point we inserted or the point that used to be right before  $A$ .  If it visits the point we inserted, then the marker will skip  $A$  as the point we inserted is labeled  $2$  and therefore the new labeling is an  $n$ -bad labeling.  If it visits the point that used to be right before  $A$  then it must move one point forward (as it already visited that point the first time around and thus cannot make the same move again) and visit the point we inserted at which it will skip  $A$  and so the new labeling is an  $n$ -bad labeling.</details>

Thus, we have showed that inserting a point right before  $A$  in an  $n-1$ -good labeling that is labeled the same as the point right before it will results in a unique  $n$ -bad labeling.  Therefore, our mapping is surjective.  Combining this results with our proof of injectivity above, we see that this mapping is one to one and therefore the number of  $n-1$ -good labelings, which is  $a_{n-1}$  is equal to the number of  $n$ -bad labelings.  However, we see that any labeling of  $n$  points must either be  $n$ -good or  $n$ -bad and there are  $2$  choices of labels for each of the  $n$  points so there are  $2^n$  possible labelings in total.  Thus, the number of  $n$ -good labelings plus  $n$ -bad labelings is equal to  $2^n$ , but the number of  $n$ -bad labelings is  $a_{n-1}$  and the number of  $n$ -good labelings is  $a_n$  so  $a_n+a_{n-1}=2^n$  as desired.   $\blacksquare$</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Classify paths by the number of points they visit twice (which we'll call "good" points), where we say  $A$  is visited "twice" if in addition to starting and ending there the path lands on  $A$ . First, we'll show that for a fixed set of  $G$  good points, there are  $2^{G}$  valid paths that visit exactly that set of points twice if that set includes  $A$ , and  $2^{G - 1}$  otherwise. 

Consider a set of good points which includes  $A$  - denote it by  $(A = p_1, p_2, p_3, \dots, p_{G})$ . Each valid path is made up of a pair of paths between each pair  $(p_i, p_{i + 1})$  - this pair of paths must intersect only at  $p_i$  and  $p_{i + 1}$ . It is easy to see that    there is only one such pair of non-intersecting paths - the paths make steps of size  $1, 2, 2, \dots, 1/2$  and  $2, 2, 2, \dots, 2/1$  where the identity of the last step depends on the parity of the length of the path. For each pair of neighboring good points, we can execute either of these paths first and the other second, giving  $2^G$  paths in all. 

Otherwise, if  $A$  is not good, let  $(p_1 \ne A, p_2, \dots, p_{G})$  be our set. Each valid path consists of a path from  $A$  to  $p_1$ , a pair of paths from  $p_i$  to  $p_{i + 1}$  for  $1 \le i \le G - 1$ , a path from  $p_G$  to  $p_1$ , and a path from  $p_G$  to  $A$ . Each of the  $G - 1$  paths from  $p_i$  to  $p_{i + 1}$  where  $1 \le i \le G - 1$  again gives two possibilities. It remains only to find the number of ways to construct a path from  $p_1$  to  $A$  and a path from  $p_G$  to  $A$  that don't intersect a third path from  $p_G$  to  $p_1$ . Treating the two paths from  $p_G$  to  $A$  and from  $A$  to  $p_1$  as a single path, this is equivalent to constructing a pair of non-intersecting paths from  $p_G$  to  $p_1$ ; however, we cannot execute them in any order - we must include  $A$  in our first pass, and exactly one of the two non-intersecting paths does this. Then in all, we have  $2^{G - 1}$  paths, as claimed. 

The only restriction on sets of good points is that no two be consecutive; given a line of  $a$  items, there are easily \[\binom{a - b + 1}{b}\] ways to choose  $b$  of them with no two consecutive. Together with casework on whether or not we include  $A$  as a good point, the number of paths in all is \[a_n = 2\sum_{k \ge 0}{\binom{n - 2 - k}{k}2^k} + \sum_{k \ge 1}{\binom{n - k}{k}2^{k - 1}} + \frac{1 - (-1)^n}{2} \; \; \; \; (*)\] where the final term is to account for the fact that the null set is a valid configuration of good points iff  $n$  is odd. Now notice \begin{align*} \sum_{k}{\binom{n - k}{k}x^k} &= [y^n]\left(\sum_{n}{y^n\sum_{k}{\binom{n - k}{k}x^k}}\right)  &= [y^n]\left(\sum_{k}{x^k\sum_{n}{\binom{n - k}{k}y^n}}\right)   &= [y^n]\left(\sum_{k}{x^k\frac{y^{2k}}{(1 - y)^{k + 1}}}\right)  &=  [y^n]\left(\frac{1}{1 - y} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \frac{xy^2}{1 - y}}\right)  &= [y^n]\left(\frac{1/3}{1 + y} + \frac{2/3}{1 - 2y} \right) = \frac{2^n + (-1)^n}{3}\end{align*} when  $x = 2$ . It's easy now to evaluate  $(*)$  explicity; it becomes \[\frac{2^{n + 1} - (-1)^{n + 1}}{3}\] so that  $a_{n - 1} + a_n = 2^n$ , as desired.</details>

Label each point with the number of times the marker is on it not counting the starting position. Every point must have the marker at some point because otherwise the move from the point before it to the point after it would be made twice. Hence, every point has 1 or 2 since the marker goes around the circle twice. Also, we can't have two consecutive points both labelled 2, because that would mean that on both times around the circle the marker moved from one point to the other, which is a repeated move.

Now, we will split into two cases, first if  $A$  is labelled 2. Given any two consecutive 2-labelled points, the paths the marker takes the first and second time must intersect only at those two points and not in between. Hence, two consecutive points in between the two points cannot both be on one path, because the other path will have to contain one of them otherwise. This results in two ways to get from the first 2-point to the next. Either move the marker by 1, 2, 2, ... or by 2, 2, 2, ... and making the appropriate move at the end to get onto the second 2-point. Whichever way the marker goes the first time, it must go the other way the second time. Hence, if there are  $k$  points labelled with 2 on the circle, there are  $2^k$  paths. The number of ways to choose  $k$  non-consecutive points including  $A$  on the circle is  $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ , so there are  $\sum_{k=1}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}2^k$  ways.

For the second case,  $A$  is not labelled with 2. The argument for consecutive 2-points that do not have  $A$  between them is the same. We will show that there is exactly one way to move between consecutive 2-points that have  $A$  between them. Suppose that the closest two 2-points to  $A$  are  $B$  and  $C$ , where  $B\rightarrow A\rightarrow C$  is in the clockwise direction. Merge the path from  $A$  to  $C$  at the start and the path from  $B$  to  $A$  at the end. This creates two paths from  $B$  to  $C$  that cannot intersect. As in the last case, there are two such choices for one of these paths. However, one of them must pass through  $A$ , so this uniquely determines the other path as well. Hence, there will be  $2^{k-1}$  paths if there are  $k$  2-points. Since there are  $\binom{n-k}{k}$  ways to choose  $k$  non-consecutive points not including  $A$  on the circle, there are  $\sum_{k=1}\binom{n-k}{k}2^{k-1}$  ways for this case.

For the final case, we consider if there are none of the points are labelled with 2. If this happens, every point is visited exactly once. The marker travels a total distance of  $2n$ . If every point is visited exactly once, then it makes exactly  $n$  moves, so on each of those moves it must travel a distance of 2. However, if  $n$  is even this obviously brings it back to  $A$ , but if  $n$  is odd then this becomes a valid path.

So if  $n$  is odd then  $a_n=1+\sum_{k=1}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}2^k+\binom{n-k}{k}2^{k-1}$  and if  $n$  is even then  $a_n=\sum_{k=1}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}2^k+\binom{n-k}{k}2^{k-1}$ . Substituting the sums into  $a_n+a_{n-1}=2^n$ , we find an identity that can be easily proven by induction.

Imagine the counter is moving along the set  $S = \{0, 1, \dots, 2n\}$  instead, starting at  $0$  and ending at  $2n$ , in jumps of length  $1$  and  $2$ . We can then record the sequence of moves as a matrix of the form \[ 	\begin{bmatrix} 		p_0 & p_1 & p_2 & \dots & p_{n-1} & p_n  		p_n & p_{n+1} & p_{n+2} & \dots & p_{2n-1} & p_{2n} 	\end{bmatrix} \] where  $p_i$  denotes whether  $i$  was used; in particular,  $p_0 = p_{2n} = 1$ . (Note that the upper-right and lower-left entries are equal.) Then, the problem amounts to finding the number of such matrices which avoid the contiguous submatrices \[ 	\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} 	\qquad 	\begin{bmatrix} 0  0 \end{bmatrix} 	\qquad 	\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1  1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \] which correspond to forbidding jumps of length greater than  $2$ , repeating a length  $2$  jump and repeating a length  $1$  jump.

We will for now ignore the boundary conditions. Instead we say a  $2 \times m$  matrix is *silver* ( $m \ge 2$ ) if it avoids the three shapes above. We can classify silver matrices into two shapes:  
- *type B matrices*, of the shape  $\begin{bmatrix} 	1 & \dots & 1  	0 & \dots & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ , and
- *type C matrices*, of the shape  $\begin{bmatrix} 	1 & \dots & 0  	0 & \dots & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ .
 We let  $b_m$  and  $c_m$  denote matrices of each type, of size  $2 \times m$ , and claim the following two recursions for  $m \ge 4$ : \begin{align*} 	b_m &= c_{m-1} + b_{m-2} + c_{m-2}  	c_m &= b_{m-1} + b_{m-2} + c_{m-2}. \end{align*} We prove the first recursion since the second is analogous. Consider the second column of a type B matrix. If it is  $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0  1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$  then we find a type C matrix, giving  $c_{m-1}$ . If it is  $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1  1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$  then the third column must be either  $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0  1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$  or  $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1  0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ , and we get a count of  $b_{m-2} + c_{m-2}$ .

Using this recursion, the first few values are \[ 	\begin{array}{rrrrrrrr} 		n  & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 &  6 &  7 &  8  \hline 		b_n & 0 & 2 & 2 & 6 & 10 & 22 & 42  		c_n & 1 & 1 & 3 & 5 & 11 & 21 & 43 	\end{array} \] and a calculation gives  $b_n = \frac{2^{n-1} - 2(-1)^{n-1}}{3}$ ,  $c_n = \frac{2^{n-1} + (-1)^{n-1}}{3}$ .

We now relate  $a_n$  to  $b_m$  and  $c_m$ . Observe that a matrix as described in the problem is a silver matrix of one of two forms: \[ 	\begin{bmatrix} 		1 & p_1 & p_2 & \dots & p_{n-1} & 0  		0 & p_{n+1} & p_{n+2} & \dots & p_{2n-1} & 1 	\end{bmatrix} 	\qquad 	\text{or}\qquad 	\begin{bmatrix} 		1 & p_1 & p_2 & \dots & p_{n-1} & 1  		1 & p_{n+1} & p_{n+2} & \dots & p_{2n-1} & 1 	\end{bmatrix}. \] There are  $c_{n+1}$  matrices of the first form and  $2b_{n-1} + 2c_{n-1}$  matrices of the second form, thus calculation gives the result \[ a_n = c_{n+1} + 2b_{n-1} + 2c_{n-1} 	= \frac{2^{n+1} + (-1)^{n+1}}{3}. \]

**Lemma:** Every point is hit at least once in the sequence of moves.**Proof:**If a point  $P_i$  wasn't hit the first time around, that means that a move of length 2 was performed from  $P_{i-1}$ . In the second revolution, if  $P_{i-1}$  is hit, then a move of length 1 must be performed, meaning  $P_i$  will be hit. Otherwise,  $P_{i-1}$  was skipped (i.e. a move of length 2 was performed from  $P_{i-2}$ ) which will still result in  $P_i$  being hit.

As a corollary, this means that any sequence of moves which skipped  $A$  on its first revolution is a valid sequence. 

Now, consider a circle of  $n$  points, and assign each point a number - either 1 or 2. Consider the move sequence: If a point has not been hit yet, move the amount of steps its number dictates. Otherwise, move the remaining move. As each point is hit during the sequence of moves, all  $2^n$  of these numberings will create different move sequences.

Suppose  $a_n=k$  of these sequences end up landing on  $A$  after exactly 2 revolutions. So,  $2^n-k$  of them failed. Now, consider a circle of size  $n+1$ , with numbers also assigned to all of the points.

We define the  $n$ -subgame of such a circle to be the result obtained from taking a circle of size  $n$  with the first  $n$  labels from the current circle.

If the  $n$ -subgame skips  $A$  on its first revolution, that means that it will skip the point before  $A$  in the  $n+1$  circle, so the point before  $A$  will be hit on the second revolution. This means that it must be numbered with a 1.

If the  $n$ -subgame hits  $A$  on its first revolution, then it hits the point before  $A$  on its first revolution in the  $n+1$  circle. If we label the point with 2, then  $A$  will be skipped for the first revolution, and this must be a valid sequence of moves. On the other hand, if we label it with a 1, then we don't affect the result of the  $n$ -subgame. So, if the  $n$ -subgame yielded a good sequence of moves, then we will end up on the point before  $A$ , causing this to be a bad sequence of moves. However, if the  $n$ -subgame was bad, then this results in hitting  $A$  on the second revolution, so this is a good sequence.

To recap, if the  $n$ -subgame is good, then we can only number the last point with a 1, and if it is bad, then we can number it with 1 or 2. (recall all subgames in the first case were good by lemma.) So,  $a_{n+1}=k+2(2^n-k)=2^{n+1}-k$  as desired.

Let \(B\) be the point directly counterclockwise to \(A\). **Claim:** We land on each point either once or twice. *Proof.* If we never land on a point, then we jump over it twice. \(\blacksquare\) Consider a circle with \(n\) points and a marker labeled \(A\), and assign each point either the number \(1\) or the number \(2\); this may be done in \(2^n\) ways. Then proceed around the circle starting from \(A\), such that the first time the marker reaches a certain point labeled \(i\), it moves \(i\) points forward. (If it reaches a point labeled \(i\) a second time, its only option is to move forward \(3-i\) points.) - The paths where we reach the point \(A\) the second time around biject with the \(a_n\) ways to advance around a circle with \(n\) points. - If we do not reach the point \(A\) the second time around, then we must have jumped over \(A\) from \(B\). Just delete the point \(B\) completely; it is easy to see these paths bijects with the \(a_{n-1}\) ways to advance around a circle with \(n-1\) points. Hence \(a_n+a_{n-1}=2^n\) as needed.

Notice that the marker must arrive at each point at least once because otherwise, it jumps over that point twice, which is not possible since that would be using the same move twice. Furthermore, if we arrive at a point $\geq 3$ times, then we use the jump $2$ or jump $1$ moves twice. Hence, each point is reached by the marker once or twice. Next we establish a bijection between $a_{n-1}$ and $a_n$ . Label each point with either $1$ or $2$ , and there are $2^n$ ways to do this. For each point, when it is reached the first time, the marker performs the move on the label, and the second time, it performs the move not on the label. We divide these $2^n$ ways of labeling into two groups: one group for those where the marker reaches $A$ twice, and another for when it reaches $A$ once. For the former group of labelings, we see that they biject to the $a_n$ ways to advance around a $n$ point circle. For the latter group of labelings, we see that they biject to the $a_{n-1}$ ways to advance around a $n-1$ point circle, because the move from $A-1$ to $A+1$ is fixed, hence the remaining $n-1$ points biject to $a_{n-1}$ ways. Therefore, $a_{n-1} + a_n = 2^n$ for all $n$ , as desired.

Assign the points numbers  $1,2,\dots,n$  modulo  $n$ . Within the context of the set of moves, let the points be enumerated as  $1,2,\dots,n,n+1,n+2,\dots,2n,2n+1$ . Clearly any interval  $[a,a+1]$  is contained within exactly one move in a particular sequence of moves.

Define a *brick road* as a collection of two sequences of moves going from  $1\to n+1$  composed such that no two collections of moves contain the same particular individual move  $a\to b$ . Let the number of brick roads be  $b_n$ . Observe that

    
- $b_1=0$ ,
- $b_2=2$ ,
- Let index  $i+1>1$  denote the first instance of the two sequences agreeing. If  $i+1=n+1$  then we have  $2$  cases for  $b_n$ . Else, we get  $2b_{n-i}$  for  $i>1$ . Thus  $b_n=2\cdot [1+\sum_{1<i<n}b_{n-i}] $ .
- Counting, we get  $b_3=2,b_4=6,b_5=10,b_6=22,b_7=42,\dots$ . We claim in general that  $b_n = 2\cdot \frac{2^{n-1}-(-1)^{n-1}}{3}$ . This holds by induction, since then
    \[b_n = 2\cdot \left[1+2\cdot \frac{2^{n-2}-\frac 32-\frac 12(-1)^{n-1}}{3}\right] = 2\cdot \left[1+\frac{2^{n-1}-3-(-1)^{n-1}}{3}\right] = 2\cdot \frac{2^{n-1}-(-1)^{n-1}}{3}.\]

Then  $a_n$  is simply  $b_n$  plus the number of sequences of moves from  $1\to 2n+1$  which include  $n\to n+2$ . Now, observe there are a number of types of this: if  $1\to 2$  is also one of the moves and so is  $2n\to 2n+1$ , this is simply  $b_{n-2}$ . If  $1\to 2$  is a move and  $2n-1\to 2n+1$  is a move, this is  $\frac 12 b_{n-1}$ . The same holds if  $1\to 3$  is a move and  $2n\to 2n+1$  is a move. So far we have then counted  $b_n+b_{n-1}+b_{n-2}$  sequences.

Now, suppose  $1\to 3,n\to n+2,2n-1\to 2n+1$  are all moves. View the complete sequence of moves as a brick road. By selecting the first point at which the two sequences agree, we count  $\frac 12\sum_{1<i<n}b_{n-i}$  possibilities. If there exists no such point, then  $n$  must be odd, thus we count  $\frac 12+\frac 12(-1)^{n-1}$  additional possible moves. Hence
\[a_n = 2\cdot \frac{2^{n-1}+2^{n-2}+2^{n-3}-(-1)^{n-1}}{3} + \frac{2^{n-2}-\frac 32-\frac 12(-1)^{n-1}}{3}+\tfrac 12+\tfrac 12(-1)^{n-1}=\]
\[\frac{7\cdot 2^{n-2}+2^{n-2}-\frac 32-\frac 52(-1)^{n-1}}{3}+\tfrac 12+\tfrac 12(-1)^{n-1} = \frac{2^{n+1}-(-1)^{n+1}}{3}.\]
The problem is now dead because
\[a_n+a_{n-1}=\frac{3\cdot 2^n}{3}=2^n.\]

We first do some work to write $a_n$ in terms of a few simpler sequences. Observe that since our first move is from $A$ , we either move once or twice from $A$ . If we move twice from $A$ , we can view the sequence of moves as a pair of two moves, each of length $n$ , such that no move from the same point is the same. From here, we can discard the circle entirely and instead view the moves in terms of two horizontal bars filled with blocks of length 1 or 2 such that no two blocks are at the same length and the same spot. Here's an example: [asy] size(150); draw((0,0)--(6,0)--(6,1)--(0,1)--cycle); draw((0,2)--(6,2)--(6,3)--(0,3)--cycle); draw((1,0)--(1,1)); draw((2,0)--(2,1)); draw((4,0)--(4,1)); draw((2,2)--(2,3)); draw((3,2)--(3,3)); draw((5,2)--(5,3)); [/asy] Let the number of ways to fill a pair of bars, both with length $n$ , be $b_n$ . We will do the recursion work later. Now suppose we move once from $A$ . If we let the point counterclockwise from $A$ be $B$ , then it is clear that on the first cycle around the circle we reach $B$ , then move two points forward from there, and after that move to $A$ . Once again, we can discard the circle and view it in terms of bars, but this time the bars are offset from each other. [asy] size(150); draw((0,0)--(6,0)--(6,1)--(0,1)--cycle); draw((1,2)--(7,2)--(7,3)--(1,3)--cycle); draw((1,0)--(1,1)); draw((2,0)--(2,1)); draw((4,0)--(4,1)); draw((3,2)--(3,3)); draw((5,2)--(5,3)); [/asy] [asy] size(150); fill((4,0)--(4,1)--(6,1)--(6,0)--cycle,red); fill((4,2)--(4,3)--(6,3)--(6,2)--cycle,red); draw((0,0)--(6,0)--(6,1)--(0,1)--cycle); draw((1,2)--(7,2)--(7,3)--(1,3)--cycle); draw((1,0)--(1,1)); draw((2,0)--(2,1)); draw((4,0)--(4,1)); draw((3,2)--(3,3)); draw((4,2)--(4,3)); draw((6,2)--(6,3)); [/asy] In the examples above, the upper example is valid, but the lower is not since the two red blocks are the same length at the same spot. Let the number of ways to fill these two bars of length $n$ be $c_n$ . It is clear that $$ a_n=b_n+c_{n-1}. $$ Finally, introduce the sequence $(d_n)$ , which counts the number of ways to fill two bars: one of length $n$ , and the other of length $n-1$ . Here's an example: [asy] size(150); draw((0,0)--(6,0)--(6,1)--(0,1)--cycle); draw((0,2)--(5,2)--(5,3)--(0,3)--cycle); draw((1,0)--(1,1)); draw((2,0)--(2,1)); draw((4,0)--(4,1)); draw((2,2)--(2,3)); draw((3,2)--(3,3)); [/asy] Now that we've defined everything, it's time to do the recursion work. First consider $c_n$ . Call the bar which is offset to the right the "right bar" and the other bar the "left bar". Consider the following cases:**Case 1:** The first block in the left bar is a block of length 1. Then we clearly have $d_n$ ways to fill the remaining blocks.**Case 2:** The first block in the left bar is a block of length 2, and the first in the right bar is of length 1. Then we clearly have $d_{n-1}$ ways to fill the remaining blocks.**Case 3:** The first blocks in the left and right bars are both of length 2. Then we have $c_{n-2}$ ways to fill the remaining blocks. Hence we have the recursion $$ c_n=c_{n-2}+d_n+d_{n-1}. $$ Now we establish a relationship between $b_n$ and $d_n$ . By inspection, we can see that in one of the bars, the rightmost block is of length 1, and in the other the rightmost block is of length 2 (anything else breaks the condition). If we delete/ignore the rightmost blocks, we then get one bar of length $n-1$ and another of $n-2$ . Since $d_n$ doesn't count alignment, but there are two distinct possiblities for orientation after deleting the rightmost blocks, we establish $b_n=2d_{n-1}$ . Now we compute $b_n$ . Consider the leftmost distance along the block, except from the very left of the block, where two blocks both end (this must exist, since two blocks both end at the right edge of the bar). Here, this distance is marked by the red line: [asy] size(150); draw((0,0)--(6,0)--(6,1)--(0,1)--cycle); draw((0,2)--(6,2)--(6,3)--(0,3)--cycle); draw((1,0)--(1,1)); draw((2,0)--(2,1)); draw((4,0)--(4,1)); draw((2,2)--(2,3)); draw((3,2)--(3,3)); draw((5,2)--(5,3)); draw((2,-1)--(2,4),red); [/asy] It is not hard to see that it is impossible for this distance to be 1, and for any (integer) distance in $[2,n]$ there is exactly two ways to fill in the blocks to the left of this distance. Hence we have the recursion: $$ b_n=2b_{n-2}+2b_{n-3}+\cdots+2b_0. $$ Comparing $b_n$ and $b_{n-1}$ and subtracting, we obtain $$ b_n-b_{n-1}=2b_{n-2} \implies b_n=b_{n-1}+2b_{n-2}. $$ Further, it's not hard to compute $b_0=1$ (there is one way to fill in the empty bars: doing nothing), and $b_1=0$ (if necessary, you can also compute a bit more). From here, simple induction is sufficient to show that $$ b_n=\frac{2}{3}(2^{n-1}+(-1)^n), $$ which also gives $$ d_n=\frac{1}{3}(2^n-(-1)^n). $$ Using this, we can verify the identity $$ b_n+b_{n-1}=2^{n-1}, $$ as well as $$ d_n+d_{n-1}=2^{n-1} \implies c_n=c_{n-2}+2^{n-1}. $$ Further, we can get $c_0=c_1=1$ , so \begin{align*} c_{2m}&=2^{2m-1}+2^{2m-3}+\cdots+2^1+1 c_{2m+1}&=2^{2m}+2^{2m-2}+\cdots+2^2+1. \end{align*} We're actually done now, since \begin{align*} a_{n-1}+a_n&=b_n+b_{n-1}+c_{n-1}+c_{n-2} &=2^{n-1}+2^{n-2}+2^{n-3}+\cdots+2^2+2^1+1+1 &=2^{n-1}+2^{n-1}=2^n.\quad \blacksquare \end{align*}

Here is what I think is a repaired version of the solution in post #39. (Note that in my write-up, the matrix has one extra redundant column compared to the notation in fclvbfm934's post).

Record the sequence of moves as a matrix of the form \[ \begin{bmatrix} p_0 & p_1 & p_2 & \dots & p_{n-1} & p_n  p_n & p_{n+1} & p_{n+2} & \dots & p_{2n-1} & p_{2n} \end{bmatrix} \] where  $p_i = 1$  if the point  $i$  was visited by the counter, and  $p_i = 0$  if the point was not visited by the counter. Note that  $p_0 = p_{2n} = 1$  and the upper-right and lower-left entries are equal. Then, the problem amounts to finding the number of such matrices which avoid the contiguous submatrices \[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \qquad \begin{bmatrix} 0  0 \end{bmatrix} \qquad \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1  1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \] which correspond to forbidding jumps of length greater than  $2$ , repeating a length  $2$  jump and repeating a length  $1$  jump.
If we focus on just the three possible column vectors that appear, say \[ \mathbf u \coloneqq \begin{bmatrix} 1  0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf v \coloneqq \begin{bmatrix} 0  1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf w \coloneqq \begin{bmatrix} 1  1 \end{bmatrix} \] then we can instead describe valid matrices as sequences of  $n+1$  such column vectors, where no two column vectors are adjacent, and where the boundary condition is that  
- either we start with  $\mathbf u$  and end with  $\mathbf v$ , or
- either we start with  $\mathbf w$  and end with  $\mathbf w$ .
 Let  $x_n$  and  $y_n$  denote the number of such  $2 \times (n+1)$  matrices. (Hence  $a_n = x_n + y_n$ .) But owing to the symmetry of the setup with  $\mathbf u$ ,  $\mathbf v$ ,  $\mathbf w$ , we could instead view  $x_n$  and  $y_n$  as the number of  $2 \times (n+1)$  matrices for a fixed starting first column whose final column is the same/different. So we have the recursions \begin{align*} x_{n+1} &= x_n + y_n  y_{n+1} &= 2x_n. \end{align*} We also have that \[ 2x_n + y_n = 2^n \] which may either be proved directly from the recursions (using  $x_0=1$  and  $y_0=0$ ), or by noting the left-hand side counts the total number of sequences of  $n+1$  column vectors with no restrictions on the final column at all (in which case there are simply  $2$  choices for each of the  $n$  columns after the first one). Thus, \begin{align*} a_{n+1} + a_n &= (x_{n+1} + y_{n+1}) + (x_n + y_n)  &= \left( (x_n + y_n) + 2x_n \right) + (x_n + y_n)  &= 2(2x_n + y_n) = 2^{n+1} \end{align*} as needed.

The only cases that don't fall into  $a_n$  are when the last jump skips over the original point  $A$ . Let  $A$  be preceded by  $A'$ , which is preceded by  $A''$ . In this case, there are two subcases:

First, if we reached  $A'$  the first time around and moved one to  $A$ , then reached  $A'$  the second time around and jumped over  $A$ . In this case, merging  $A'$  into  $A$  and removing the first jump reduces bijectively to the cases for  $n - 1$  where we reach  $A$  twice during the process.

Second, if we skipped  $A'$  the first time around and the second time around we jumped over  $A$ . In this case, we always reach  $A''$  in the first go around. Thus, if we merge  $A$  into  $A'$ , endowing  $A'$  with the initial action of  $A$ , then this bijects into the cases for  $n - 1$  where we skip  $A$  during the process by reach  $A$  after the second loop.

Thus, since we have accounted for all cases, we have  $a_{n-1} +a_n = 2^n$  as desired.

sketch (similar to #43):
label the points from 1 to n in clockwise order, with A being the point with label 1.
note that each sequence of moves can be expressed in a binary string of n digits, where the ith digit denotes whether the marker moves one or two moves when first reaching the ith point (for instance, a 0 in the third digit denotes that the marker moves to the fourth point when first landing on the third point, and vice versa). obviously, if a marker reaches a point twice, it will take the opposite move of what it did when it reached the point the first time

it is provable that the marker lands on each point at least once, which implies that any sequence of moves that lands on A after two cycles has an unique binary string representation of length n
on the contrary, any binary string of length n represents a sequence of moves that either lands on A after two cycles, or jumps from point n to point 2 after passing through A the second time.
clearly, the number of binary strings fulfilling the first scenario is equal to a_n, so it suffices to prove that the number of binary strings of length n fulfilling the second scenario is equal to a_n-1, or the number of binary strings of length n-1 that represent a successful sequence of moves

caseworking on the last two digits gives that for any binary string s of length n-2:
- the concatenated strings s01 and s10 always result in a successful sequence;
- exactly one of the strings s00 and s0 result in a successful sequence;
- and similarly, exactly one of the strings s11 and s1 result in a successful sequence.

this result directly implies a_(n-1) + a_n = 2^n, so we are done.

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer.  There are  $\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$  marks, each with a black side and a white side, arranged into an equilateral triangle, with the biggest row containing  $n$  marks.  Initially, each mark has the black side up.  An *operation* is to choose a line parallel to the sides of the triangle, and flipping all the marks on that line.  A configuration is called *admissible* if it can be obtained from the initial configuration by performing a finite number of operations.  For each admissible configuration  $C$ , let  $f(C)$  denote the smallest number of operations required to obtain  $C$  from the initial configuration.  Find the maximum value of  $f(C)$ , where  $C$  varies over all admissible configurations.
solution_md:
Here is another approach to obtain the upper bound on the maximum value of  $f$  (which is probably equivalent to the approaches described above):

Suppose a configuration  $\mathcal{D}$  can be arranged in  $m$  operations using a sequence of operations  $S$ . There are a total of  $3n$  possible operations so this leaves  $3n-m$  operations not in  $S$ . If we label the sides of the triangle as  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$ , then there are  $n$  operations which act in lines parallel to each of  $A$ ,  $B$ , and  $C$ . In particular, of the  $3n-m$  operations unused,  $x \ge \left \lceil \frac{3n-m}{3} \right\rceil$  of them are parallel to a specific side, WLOG  $A$ . Therefore, we could also obtain  $\mathcal{D}$  by applying the  $n$  operations parallel to  $A$  and then the  $3n-m$  operations unused in  $S$ ; however, we can do even better: each of the  $x$  operations not in  $S$  parallel to side  $A$  are done twice in this process; we can therefore avoid ever doing them at all. Then:
\begin{align*}
f(\mathcal{D}) &\le \min(m, n + (3n-m) - 2x) 
&\le \min\left(m, 4n - m - 2\left\lceil \frac{3n-m}{3} \right\rceil\right) 
&= \min \left(m, 2n - m + 2\left \lfloor \frac{m}{3} \right \rfloor \right)
\end{align*}

The last statement is maximized for  $n = \left\lfloor \frac{3}{2}n \right\rfloor$ , giving  $f(\mathcal{D}) \le \left \lfloor \frac{3}{2}n \right \rfloor$ .

This is optimal for  $n \equiv 0, 1 \pmod 4$  and one higher than optimal for  $n \equiv 2, 3 \pmod 4$ .

<details><summary>To decrease the bound by 1 in the latter two cases:</summary>Decreasing the bound by  $1$  for  $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$  is similar to the process for  $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$  so we focus on  $2$ .

So for  $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ , suppose there is a configuration which at a minimum requires  $3n/2$  operations, with a set  $S'$  of operations witnessing this; in other words,  $S'$  is a function on the triangle. Using the notation of previous users, let it have  $a_o$  operations which are along odd-length rows parallel to side  $A$ ,  $a_e$  operations which are along even-length rows parallel to  $A$ , and define  $b_o$ ,  $b_e$ ,  $c_o$ ,  $c_e$  similarly. Then  $a_o + a_e + b_o + b_e + c_o + c_e = 3n/2$ .

As discussed in previous posts, the set of operations of toggling all even-length rows in all three directions is an identity. Denote the function corresponding to this by  $E$ . Likewise, toggling the states of all rows parallel to two distinct directions is also an identity. Denote the functions corresponding to these by  $P_{A,B}, P_{B,C}, P_{C,A}$ .

If we apply  $E \circ S'$ , we have the same configuration but used  $a_o + (n/2 - a_e) + b_o + (n/2 - b_e) + c_o + (n/2 - c_e)$  operations. So we assume instead that  $a_o + b_o + c_o \ge a_e + b_e + c_e$ ; in fact, due to parity, this implies that  $a_o + b_o + c_o > a_e + b_e + c_e$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>There are 3n possible moves.  I will call them  $a_1, a_2, ..., a_n, b_1, b_2, ..., b_n, c_1, c_2, ..., c_n$ .  The a's will be slanting upwards, the b's will slanting downwards, and the c's are horizontal.  The index indicates the number of markers in the row.

Clearly, the moves are all commutative, and they are all their own inverses.  So we can express any series of moves just as a sum of the component moves.

It would be nice if the moves were all independent (i.e., we could apply any number of them and they would never cancel).  The answer would just be 3n.  Unfortunately, they're not.  For instance, if you apply all a and all b moves, or all even indexed moves, you get back to start (long series of moves can be simplified by using these "identities").  In other words, you can actually form some moves using other moves (for instance, you could form any b move by applying all a moves and all the other b moves).  In this sense, the 3n moves contain "extra" information and are "redundant".

As a lemma, I will show that there are exactly 3 "extra" moves.  More specifically, I will show that you can choose 3 moves that you can form from the other 3n-3, but you can't choose 4 that you can form from the other 3n-4.  If you know linear algebra, if we were to form a matrix of the operations where columns represent markers and rows represent moves and worked modulo 2, the matrix would have rank 3n-3.

It is easy to find 3: take  $b_1$ ,  $c_1$ , and  $c_2$ .  For  $b_1$ , apply all of the a moves and all of the other b moves.  For  $c_2$ , apply all of the other even indexed moves.  And for  $c_1$ , apply all even indexed b moves and all other odd indexed a and c moves.

Now assume you can find 4 that can be derived from the other 3n-4.  If these four are (WLOG)  $a_i$ ,  $b_j$ ,  $c_k$ , and  $c_l$ , look at the formula for  $a_i$ .  It can't have only a and b moves, as this would require all of them, and  $b_j$  is missing.  So there is a c move  $c_m$  in this formula.  We can now solve for  $c_m$  in terms of  $a_i$ , and find  $b_j$ ,  $c_k$ , and  $c_l$  using  $a_i$  instead of  $c_m$  if necessary.  Basically we can swap out our a move with a c move.  We can do the same thing if we have (WLOG) two b moves and two c moves.

So we can a set of four "redundant" moves, three of which are c moves.  Two of them must have the same parity:  $c_j$  and  $c_k$ , where j<k.  We are able to form  $c_j$  without using  $c_k$ .

Take any marker (call it M1) in the  $c_j$  row.  This must be flipped exactly once, either by an a row or a b row.  The marker directly below M1 (call it M2) in the  $c_k$  row must be flipped an even number of times, as it must stay black, and  $c_k$  can't be flipped, so the a and b row passing through M2 are either both flipped or both not flipped.

But this causes trouble in the  $c_{(j+k)/2}$  row.  This row has two corners of the rhombus whose other corners are M1 and M2 and whose sides are a and b rows.  An odd number of these sides must be flipped (odd from M1, even from M2).  Thus, the other corners of the rhombus will have different sides facing up (whether  $c_{(j+k)/2}$  is applied or not), so we can't wind up with only move  $c_j$ .  This is a contradiction, so the lemma is true.

So we can only have thee independent "identities" (a bunch of moves that sum to zero).  An example of some 3 would be: The sum of all a's and b's is zero, the sum of all b's and c's is zero, and the sum of all even indexed moves is zero (by zero, I mean the identity).  The lemma guarantees that there are no other independent ones, though we can derive a few more from these three (all a's and c's sum to zero, all odd a's and b's and even c's sum to zero, etc.)

Now take any admissible configuration and write it as a sum of moves.  These moves belong to one of six sets:  $A_O$  (all a's with odd indices),  $A_E$  (all a's with even indices),  $B_O$ ,  $B_E$ ,  $C_O$ ,  $C_E$ .  Say these sets have u, v, w, x, y, and z moves, respectively.  We know that: \[A_O+A_E=B_O+B_E=C_O+C_E\]  \[A_E+B_E+C_E=0\]  \[A_O+B_O+C_E=0\]  \[A_O+B_E+C_O=0\]  \[A_E+B_O+C_O=0\] (Here the name of any set denotes the sum of all it's elements.)  So if we have more than half of the moves in any one of these identities, we can just take the other half, giving the same configuration in fewer moves.  So the maximal one will satisfy: \[v+x+z \le \frac{1}{2}(|A_E|+|B_E|+|C_E|)=0.\]  The even sets have size  $\lfloor{n/2}\rfloor$ , so \[ v+x+z \le \lfloor{3\lfloor{n/2}\rfloor/2}\rfloor.\]  Doing similar bounds for the sums u+w+z, u+x+y, and v+w+y, (note that the odd sets have size  $\lceil{n/2}\rceil$ ), adding them all up, cleaning up the floors and ceilings, dividing by 2, and taking the floor, and cleaning up more floors and ceilings (I'm not typing all of this), you get: \[u+v+w+x+y+z \le n + 2\lfloor{n/4}\rfloor.\]  This is optimal: you can choose your u, v, w, x, y, z, to make all inequalities happy (casework on n mod 4), and any choice of the moves within their respective sets works.</details>

First, note that the base cases  $n = 1, 2, 3$  are trivial by checking to be  $1, 2, 3$ . Now note the case  $n = 4$  needs at least  $6$  to construct a black triangle with a single white mark at its center by checking. Call this size  $4$  triangle the evil triangle.

 To show the lower bound, notice we can take the top  $n$  rows of a  $n+4$  equilateral triangle to be the limiting case for  $n$  and put two evil triangles on the bottom left and bottom right, respectively: these force  $4$  new rows to be occupied since each evil subcase requires at least two rows in every direction, which is a claim easy verified.

To show the upper bound, we reparameterize the triangles in terms of their rows. Notably, we can start counting rows from each corner, and give each mark a barycentric coordinate  $(a, b, c)$  where  $a, b, c$  are integers denoting the  $i$ th row in a given direction the point lies in, and this satisfies  $a+b+c = 2n+1$  by Viviani's theorem.

Now, consider the configuration  $C$  that minimizes  $f(C)$ . We place the rows in boxes: odd rows of each direction, and even rows of each direction, to make six boxes total. Call the numbers of odd rows  $a, b, c$  and the even rows  $d, e, f$  such that  $(a, b, c)$  and  $(d, e, f)$  correspond to the same directions respectively in that order. Notice no row is operated on twice since row operations are commutative. Assume for sake of contradiction our claim is wrong, then we can construct a solution for the case one higher than our claim.

We now perform casework: for  $b = 4$ , it follows one of the quantities  $a+b+d+e, b+c+e+f, c+a+f+d$  is greater than  $n$ . In this case, invert the rows chosen in those four boxes (i.e. remove the ones chosen and choose the ones unchosen). This fixes the configuration and decreases  $f(C)$ , giving contradiction.

Now, consider the case  $b = 1$ . Like the above paragraph, we know  $a+d, b+e, c+f$  are equal to  $2k, 2k+1, 2k+1$  in some order since if any pair sums to more than  $4k+1$  then we reach a contradiction. But then  $2k+1 + 2k + 1 > 4k + 2$ , giving contradiction.

Now, for the two remaining cases, we show a lemma: the xor of all the odd rows in two directions and all the even row in a third direction, or the sum of all the even rows in all directions are both  $0$ . This result follows immediately from our earlier result via Vivani's theorem (it cannot be that all three claims are true, and it cannot be the case that two of the claims are false and one is true by parity).

Thus in the  $b = 2$  case it follows that  $\min(a+b+f, b+c+d, c+a+e, d+e+f) \geq \frac{12k+6}{4}$  so one of the triples is at least  $3k + 2$ . However inverting the three involved boxes, that total to  $6k+3$  rows and don't affect the configuration when all three are inverted, decreases the  $f(C)$ , giving contradiction.

Finally, in the  $b = 3$  it follows that  $(a+b+f)+(b+c+d) + (c+a+e) + (d+e+f) =12k+8$ . In particular, the odd/odd/even triples consist of  $\frac{n+1}{2} + \frac{n+1}{2} + \frac{n-1}{2} = 6k+5$  rows each, while the even/even/even triple consists of  $3 \cdot \frac{n-1}{2} = 6k+3$  rows. For each of the triples to avoid decreases  $f(C)$  after being inverted, it needs to satisfy either  $\leq 3k + 2$  or  $\leq 3k+1$  depending on the two cases, so it follows that  $LHS \leq 12k + 7$ , giving contradiction. 

Thus we have reached contradiction in all cases of counterexamples, proving our desired claim.

Operations are commutative and their own inverse, so every sequence of operations can be thought of as just a subset of the  $3n$  possible operations. In addition to being self-inverses, there is one more universal identity rule: performing all possible operations in one direction and all possible operations in a second direction leads back to the initial configuration.

This gives rise to an action on operation subsets for a configuration. If we have a subset of operations leading to a given admissible state  $C$ , we can take the complement of operations along two directions to find another (possibly smaller) subset of operations leading to  $C$ .

Due to this action, a minimal subset of operations for a state  $C$  cannot have more than  $n$  total operations in any two directions. Otherwise, we could take the complement in these two directions and find a smaller subset. If  $x$ ,  $y$ , and  $z$  are the numbers of operations in the three directions for a minimal subset, then:
\[
x + y + z = \frac{1}{2} \big( (x + y) + (y + z) + (z + x) \big) \leq \frac{1}{2}(n + n + n) = \frac{3n}{2}.
\]

I strongly suspect that  $\lfloor 3n/2 \rfloor$  is the maximum across all configurations, but I have not yet found a proof of this.[\hide]</details>

The tangents become circles through  $P$  tangent to the two lines.  $B,C$  become points on the two lines such that  $B',C',P$  are collinear. Since  $\angle B'A'P=\angle PBA$  and  $\angle C'A'P=\angle PCA$  are fixed, and we can assume  $A'P$  is fixed since the condition is homologous, we just want to find all lines  $B'C'$  through  $P$  fixed satisfying the condition.
The original condition is
\[
\left(\frac{PA}{XY}\right)^2+\frac{PB\cdot PC}{AB\cdot AC}=1
\]
Note that
\[
XY=XP+PY=\frac{1}{X'P}+\frac{1}{PY'}
\]
\[
AB=\frac{A'B'}{PA'\cdot PB'}
\]
and similarly
\[
AC=\frac{A'C'}{PA'\cdot PB'}.
\]
Of course  $PA=\frac{1}{PA'}$ ,  $PB=\frac{1}{PB'}$ ,  $PC=\frac{1}{PC'}$  as well.
Putting this all together, the condition becomes
\[
(\frac{PX'\cdot PY'}{PA'\cdot X'Y'})^2+\frac{PA'^2}{A'B'\cdot A'C'}=1
\]
Let the ratio of homothety that maps the smaller circle to the bigger one be  $r$ . Then  $A'X'=\frac{A'P}{r}$  and  $A'Y'=r\cdot A'P$ . This implies
\[
PX'=A'P-A'X=A'P(1-\frac{1}{r})
\]
\[
PY'=A'Y'-A'P=A'P(r-1)
\]
\[
X'Y'=AY'-AX'=A'P(r-\frac{1}{r})
\]
So
\[
\frac{PX'\cdot PY'}{PA'\cdot X'Y'}=\frac{(r-1)(r-1)}{r^2-1}=\frac{r-1}{r+1}
\]
Squaring this term and subtracting it from  $1$  yields the form of the condition
\[
\frac{A'P^2}{A'B'\cdot A'C'}=\frac{4r}{(r+1)^2}
\]


Now we claim that the line  $B'C'$  is a solution to this if  $AB'=AC'$ . Indeed, if this is true, then
\[
\frac{A'P^2}{A'B'\cdot A'C'}=\frac{A'P^2}{A'B'^2}
\]
so the equality becomes
\[
\frac{A'P}{A'B'}=\frac{2\sqrt{r}}{r+1}
\]
Now  $A'P\cdot A'Y'=A'E^2$  and  $\frac{A'Y'}{A'P}=r$ , so  $\frac{A'E'}{A'P}=\sqrt{r}$ . Then we multiply the above equation by  $\sqrt{r}$  to obtain
\[
\frac{A'E'}{A'B'}=\frac{2r}{r+1}
\]
But  $A'D'=\frac{A'E'}{r}$ , and  $A'B'=\frac{A'D'+A'E'}{2}$  because  $B'$  lying on the radical axis is the midpoint of the external tangent. Thus the result follows.

Now assume that some other  $B_2,C_2$  also satisfies the equation. Then since everything else is fixed, we must have  $A'B_2\cdot A'C_2=A'B'\cdot A'C'$ . But this is equivalent to
\[
\frac{A'B_2}{A'B'}=\frac{A'C'}{A'C_2}
\]
So  $B'C_2\parallel B_2C'$ . But this implies
\[
\frac{B'P}{PC'}=\frac{B_2P}{C_2P}
\]
So before inversion we must have had this inverse ratio as well. Since  $P$  is on a fixed line segment, the two solutions are when  $\angle A'B'C'=\angle A'C'B'$ , or equivalently, when  $AP$  bisects  $\angle CAB$ , and the reflection of this point across the midpoint of  $BC$ .</details>

An 'easy, short, and straightforward' calculation:

-Parameters: Let  $r_1$ ,  $r_2$  be the circumradii of circle  $\omega_1$ ,  $\omega_2$ , respectively. Let  $d = O_1O_2$ .

-Variable: Let  $x=PB/BC$ . Then  $PC/BC=1-x$ .

-Calculation of  $1-(AP/XY)^2 = d^2/(r_1+r_2)^2$ :
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Suppose  $r_1<r_2$ . Then the external common tangent of  $\omega_1, \omega_2$  meet at some point  $Z$ . Let  $\theta = \angle ZT_1O_1$ .  Suppose the tangent line which passes through  $X$  touches  $\omega_1$  at  $T_1$  and  $\omega_2$  at  $T_2$ . Another tangent line touches the circles at  $S_1$ ,  $S_2$ . It is well known that  $XT_1=XT_2$  (Proof by power of points:  $XT_1^2 = XA\cdot XP=XT_2^2$ ), and also  $YS_1=YS_2$ . Then by the similar triangles  $\triangle ZT_1S_1, \triangle ZXY, \triangle ZT_2S_2$ , we know that 
\[XY = (T_1S_1+T_2S_2)/2 = (ZT_1+ZT_2)\sin \theta=(r_1+r_2)\sin \theta / \tan \theta = (r_1+r_2)\cos\theta.\]

Using Heron's formula, we have 

\[(AP\cdot d /4)^2 = [O_1O_2A]^2 = s(s-d)(s-r_1)(s-r_2)=[(r_1+r_2)^2-d^2][d^2-(r_2-r_1)^2]/16\]
\[(AP)^2 =[(r_1+r_2)^2-d^2][1-(\frac{r_2-r_1}{d})^2]=[(r_1+r_2)^2-d^2](1-\sin^2\theta\]

Thererfore 

\[1-(\frac{AP}{XY})^2 = 1- \frac{(r_1+r_2)^2-d^2}{(r_1+r_2)^2} = \frac{d^2}{(r_1+r_2)^2}\]

It is similar for the case when  $r_2<r_1$ . For  $r_1=r_2$  it is also easy to verify the equation directly (without using  $\theta$ ).</details>

-Proof of  $AB\cdot AC/BC^2 = r_1r_2/d^2$ :
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Check that  $\triangle AO_1O_2$  and  $ABC$  are similar.</details>

-An equation of  $x$  is then  $x(1-x)=\frac{r_1r_2}{(r_1+r_2)^2}$ .
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>So the given equation yields that 
\[x(1-x) = [1-(\frac{AP}{XY})^2)[\frac{AB\cdot AC}{BC^2}]=\frac{r_1r_2}{(r_1+r_2)^2}\]</details>

stem_md: Given positive integers  $m$  and  $n$ , prove that there is a positive integer  $c$  such that the numbers  $cm$  and  $cn$  have the same number of occurrences of each non-zero digit when written in base ten.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Fix  $m, n$ . **Lemma:** The set of prime factors of  $\{m\cdot 10^y-n\}$  is finite.
<u>Proof:</u> Suppose it were finite, and let that set be  $S$ . Fix  $y$ . Then let  $C=(m\cdot 10^y - n)\prod_{p\in S} (p-1)$ . If  $v_p(m\cdot 10^y-n)=e$  then note  $10^C\equiv 1\pmod{p^{e+1}}$ . Thus,  $v_p(m\cdot 10^{y+C}-n)=e$  for all  $p\in S$ . But then this means that  $m\cdot 10^{y+C}-n=m\cdot 10^y-n$ , an obvious contradiction, and thus the set  $S$  is infinite as desired.  $\blacksquare$ We claim that for all  $K>0$ , we can find  $a, b, x, y$  such that  $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{m\cdot 10^y-n}{n\cdot 10^x-m}$  and  $\frac{n\cdot 10^x-m}{b}>K$ . In other words,  $\gcd (m\cdot 10^y-n, n\cdot 10^x-m)$  is arbitrarily large. But this follows since the set of prime factors of  $\{m\cdot 10^y-n\}$  is infinite for  $m, n$  fixed. 

Take  $K=\text{max}(m^2n, mn^2)$ . Then  $n\cdot 10^x-m>bmn^2$  so  $bmn<10^x$ . Similarly,  $amn<10^y$ . On the other hand, take  $c=bm\cdot 10^y+am=an\cdot 10^x+bn$ . Note  $cm=amn\cdot 10^x+bmn$  and  $cn=bmn\cdot 10^y+amn$ . Since  $10^y>amn$  and  $10^x>bnm$ , it follows that the digits of  $cm, cn$  are the same - namely the digits of  $amn$  and  $bmn$ .  $\square$</details>

The idea is to introduce a third number, k.  Then we can choose a constant c such that cm that has m's digits followed by n's digits followed by k's digits, and cn that has n's digits followed by k's digits followed by m's digits.

To get this, we want to choose c, k, r, and s such that: \[c=10^t+\frac{10^sn+k}{m} = 10^t+\frac{10^rk+m}{n}\]  Solving for k, we get: \[k=\frac{10^sn^2-m^2}{10^rm-n}\]  Choose r to be very large. In order for Alex to guarantee opening the lock, each of the  $3^3 = 27$  possible codes must be tested. Therefore, there must be at least  $27$  sequences of three consecutive button presses. <details><summary>My solution</summary>First, we find the total number of codes: since each code is 3 letters long and each letter can be one of 3 possibilities (A, B, or C), there are  $3^3 = 27$  possible codes.

Next, we determine how many codes can be tried if Alex makes  $n$  button presses, for some positive integer  $n \ge 3.$  Let the sequence of button presses be \[\overline{X_1X_2X_3\ldots X_{n-1}X_n},\] where each of the  $X_i$ s is either an A, a B, or a C. Then in this sequence, there are exactly  $n-2$  subsequences that have length 3, namely \[\overline{X_1X_2X_3}, \, \overline{X_2X_3X_4}, \, \ldots, \, \overline{X_{n-2}X_{n-1}X_n}.\] Therefore,  $n$  button presses determine  $n-2$  codes, but these codes may not all be distinct. So, if we try all 27 possible codes, we must apply at least  $27 + 2 = 29$  button presses.

Now, notice that the sequence of button presses \[\text{AAABAACABBABCACBACCBBBCBCCCAA}\] has length 29 and contains each of the 27 possible codes exactly once (this can be verified directly). We have thus shown that we must have at least 29 button presses to be able to try every possible code and that there does indeed exist a sequence of exactly 29 button presses containing every possible code. Consequently, Alex needs at least  $\boxed{29}$  button presses to guarantee opening the lock.  $\square$</details>

This is probably overkill, but instead of wasting time finding an example, you could have done this:

Let each possible combination be a vertex in some graph  $G$ . Note that any combination, with the addition of a letter after it, can lead to three other combinations, and there are exactly two other combinations that lead to those three combinations. Also note that no other combination can lead to those three combinations. Now, let  $v_1, v_2, ..., v_k$  be the longest path in  $G$ . Then,  $v_k$  can only lead to  $v_1 v_2, ..., v_{k-1}$ . Let's say that it leads to  $v_a, v_b, v_c$ , where  $a, b, c \in \{1, 2, ..., k-1\}$ . This implies that  $v_{a-1}, v_{b-1}, v_{c-1}, v_k$  are all distinct, where  $v_k = v_0$ . Then, one of  $v_a, v_b, v_c$  must  be  $v_1$ , and the path is a cycle. Since the graph is connected (we can get from one combination to another by appending the other combination to the end of the first) and no vertex in the cycle can lead to one outside of the cycle (or the longest path is contradicted), the cycle contains all the vertices in  $G$ . This requires  $3^3+3-1$  button presses.
But how do you know that  $v_k$  leads to  $v_1$ ?  Please clarify.

You use the fact (taken from what happens when you append a string) that if a vertex  $v_i$  leads to some other vertex  $v_j$ , then there are exactly two other vertices that lead to  $v_j$  and that these two vertices lead the the same set of three vertices that  $v_i$  leads to. Then, we can conclude that since  $v_k$  leads to  $v_a, v_c, v_c$ , there are exactly two other vertices that can lead to one of  $v_a, v_b, v_c$ , but  $v_{a-1}, v_{b-1}, v_{c-1}$  each lead to  $v_a, v_b, v_c$ , respectively, so  $v_{a-1}, v_{b-1}, v_{c-1}, v_k$  must constitute three distinct vertices, so one of them is equal to  $v_k$ , and hence,  $v_k$  leads to  $v_1$ .

stem_md: An infinite sequence of positive real numbers  $a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots$  is called *territorial* if for all positive integers  $i,j$  with  $i<j$ , we have  $|a_i-a_j|\ge\tfrac1j$ . Can we find a territorial sequence  $a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots$  for which there exists a real number  $c$  with  $a_i<c$  for all  $i$ ?

I will recursively define a sequence of real numbers for which for every  $n$ ,  $a_1, a_2, ..., a_n$  are territorial so it follows the infinite sequence is territorial. \

First define  $a_1 = 1, a_2 = 101$  as our base of the recursion. Now suppose for  $k \ge 3$  we have constructed a sequence  $a_1, a_2, ..., a_{k-1}$  such that for all  $i < j \le k-1$ , we have  $|a_i - a_j| \ge \frac{1}{j}$  and that  $\min(a_i) = a_1 = 1, \max(a_i) = a_2 = 101$ . I claim that we can extend the sequence to contain a real number  $a_k \in (1,101)$  such that  $|a_i - a_k| \ge \frac{1}{k}$  for all  $1 \le i < k$ . Let  $1 = b_1, b_2, ..., b_{k-1} = 2$  be a permutation of the integers  $1,2,...,k-1$  such that 
\[a_1 = a_{b_1} < a_{b_2} < ... < a_{b_{k-1}} = a_2\]
Now consider the  $k-2$  intervals of the form  $(a_{b_i}, a_{b_{i+1}})$  for  $1 \le i \le k-2$ . Note that as the sum of their lengths is  $a_2 - a_1 = 100$ , there must exist an integer  $j$  such that the interval  $(a_{b_j}, a_{b_{j+1}})$  has length at least \[\frac{100}{k-2} > \frac{100}{k} > \frac{2}{k}\]
which implies that if we let  $a_k = \frac{a_{b_j} + a_{b_{j+1}}}{2}$ , then we have  $|a_i - a_k| \ge \frac{1}{k}$  for all  $1 \le i < k$ . Note furthermore that of course we have  $a_k \in (a_1, a_2)$ . Thus with our recursive step complete we can construct an infinite territorial sequence bounded above by  $a_2 = 101$ , so the answer is yes and thus we are done.

We can find a territorial sequence for any  $c\geq2$ . We prove this by induction.

Let a \textit{partial territorial sequence} of length  $k$  be the first  $k$  terms of a territorial sequence.

For the base case, notice that for a territorial sequence  $a$ ,  $a_1$  can have any value. Thus, we can always find a partial territorial sequence of length  $1$  with all members less than  $c$ .

For the inductive step, assume that we have found a partial territorial sequence  $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots, a_k$  such that all members are less than  $c$ . We proceed to prove that some real number  $a_{k+1} < c$  must exist such that  $a_1, a_2, a_2, \dots, a_k, a_{k+1}$  is also a partial territorial sequence.

Consider the first  $k$  members of the partial territorial sequence on the number line. We choose  $a_{k+1}$  by finding a place to put  $a_{k+1}$  on the number line.

To place  $a_{k+1}$  on the number line, note that it cannot be placed within  $\frac{1}{k+1}$  units of  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{k-1},$  and  $a_k$  (otherwise we can find some  $i < k+1$  such that  $\left| a_{i} - a_{k+1} \right| < \frac{1}{k+1}$ , making the sequence non-territorial).

We now find the regions of the number line where  $a_{k+1}$  cannot be placed (call these \textit{eliminated regions}).

Each number already placed on the number line eliminates  $\frac{1}{k+1}$  units on either side (greater than and less than the number), for a total of  $\frac{2}{k+1}$ . It may be less than this if some of these eliminated areas overlap or reach outside the range  $(0, c)$ ; however,  $\frac{2}{k+1}$  is the maximum.

Since there are  $k$  numbers already placed, at most  $\frac{2k}{k+1}$  of the number line is eliminated, and so  $c - \frac{2k}{k+1}$  of the number line is guaranteed to be free to place  $a_{k+1}$ . Clearly  $\frac{2k}{k+1} < 2$ , so if  $c \geq 2$ , then  $c - \frac{2k}{k+1}$  must be positive. Hence we always have a place to place  $a_{k+1}$ .

This completes the inductive step. Because we can always append another member to a partial territorial sequence, it follows that we can repeat this process indefinitely to find an infinitely long territorial sequence with an upper bound  $c$  (as long as  $c \geq 2$ ).

stem_md:
Bunbury the bunny is hopping on the positive integers. First, he is told a positive integer  $n$ . Then Bunbury chooses positive integers  $a,d$  and hops on all of the spaces  $a,a+d,a+2d,\dots,a+2013d$ . However, Bunbury must make these choices so that the number of every space that he hops on is less than  $n$  and relatively prime to  $n$ .

A positive integer  $n$  is called *bunny-unfriendly* if, when given that  $n$ , Bunbury is unable to find positive integers  $a,d$  that allow him to perform the hops he wants. Find the maximum bunny-unfriendly integer, or prove that no such maximum exists.
solution_md:
<details><summary>My progress</summary>To convert the problem statement into the language of mathematics, we begin with a few definitions:


- For positive integers  $a, d,$  define \[H_{a, d} = \{a, a+d, a+2d, \ldots, a+2013d\},\] the set of all numbers that Bunbury hops on.
- For a positive integer  $n \neq 1,$  let \[n = (p_1^{e_1}p_2^{e_2}\ldots p_m^{e_m})(p_{m+1}^{e_{m+1}}\cdots p_k^{e_k}),\] where  $m, \, k, \, e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_k$  are positive integers,  $m \le k,$   $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$  are primes, and \[1 < p_1<p_2<\ldots<p_m<2014<p_{m+1}<\ldots<p_k.\] (The existence of  $\{p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_m\}$  is guaranteed by Lemma 1, which is proven below.)
- Given  $n,$  call an ordered pair of positive integers  $(a,d)$  \textit{bounded for  $n$ } if  $a+2013d < n,$  and call  $(a,d)$  \textit{primed for  $n$ } if  $\gcd(E, n) = 1$  for all elements  $E$  in  $H_{a,d}.$  Finally, call an ordered pair of positive integers  $(a,d)$  \textit{valid for  $n$ } if it is both bounded and primed for  $n.$  Then  $n$  is bunny-unfriendly iff no pairs  $(a,d)$  are valid. \textit{For brevity, let us exclude the numbers  $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2014$  from being bunny-unfriendly.} (This decision is valid because there are clearly larger bunny-unfriendly numbers, like  $n = 2015,$  and so by excluding those integers we are not changing the maximum bunny-unfriendly number.)
**Lemma 1: All bunny-unfriendly integers  $n$  are divisible by a prime less than  $2014.$**

Suppose that  $n$  is bunny-unfriendly. Then by definition, no ordered pairs  $(a,d)$  are valid for  $n,$  so  $(a,d) = (1,1)$  cannot be valid for  $n.$  We have \[H_{1,1} = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2014\}.\] Being that  $n>2014$  (by our assumption above), we know that  $(1,1)$  is bounded for  $n.$  Thus,  $(1, 1)$  cannot be primed for  $n$  - one of the integers in  $H_{1,1}$  must share some prime factor with  $n.$  Because all of the integers in  $H_{1, 1}$  also have their prime factors in  $H_{1, 1},$  this means that  $n$  must be divisible by a prime in  $H_{1,1}.$  Therefore, all bunny-unfriendly integers must be divisible by a prime less than 2014. (The inequality may be strict since  $2014$  is not prime.)  $\square$ (Lemma 1 also shows that there are infinitely many integers that are not bunny-unfriendly. For example, since 2017 is prime, all integers in the form  $n = 2017^x$  for some positive integer  $x$  are not bunny-unfriendly, and there are infinitely many positive integers in this form.)**Lemma 2: For positive integers  $a, d, n,$  if  $(a,d)$  is primed for  $n,$  then  $(p_1p_2\ldots p_m) | d.$**

Let  $p$  be an arbitrary element of the set  $\{p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_m\},$  and assume, for the sake of contradiction, that  $p$  does not divide  $d.$  Consider the set \[J = \{a, a+d, a+2d, \ldots, a+(p-1)d\},\] which is in fact a subset of  $H_{a,d}$  because  $p-1 < 2013.$  The difference between any two distinct elements of  $J$  is in the set  $\{d, 2d, \ldots, (p-1)d\},$  and none of these is a multiple of  $p,$  so all of the elements in  $J$  must be distinct mod  $p.$  There are exactly  $p$  elements in  $J$  and exactly  $p$  residues modulo  $p,$  so  $J$  must be a permutation of  $\{0, 1, 2, \ldots, p-1\}$  when considered mod  $p.$  In particular, one of the elements of  $J$  must be  $0$  mod  $p.$  Since  $J$  is a subset of  $H_{a, d},$  one of the elements in  $H_{a, d}$  must be divisible by  $p,$  and since  $p | n,$  this contradicts our beginning assumption that  $(a,d)$  is primed for  $n.$  Therefore,  $p$  must divide  $d.$  Since  $p$  is arbitrary, we conclude that  $d$  must be divisible by all of  $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_m,$  and so  $d$  must be divisible by  $p_1p_2\ldots p_m.$   $\square$ \bigskip

Let  $n_0 = 2013(2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdots 2011),$  where the expression in parentheses is the product of all primes less than  $2014.$  By applying the previous lemma, we will prove that  $n_0$  is bunny-unfriendly, and that it is the largest bunny-unfriendly integer whose prime factors are all less than  $2014.$  Assume to the contrary that there exists a valid ordered pair  $(a_0, d_0)$  for  $n_0.$  Since  $(a_0, d_0)$  is primed, by Lemma 2,  $d_0 = k (2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdots 2011)$  for some positive integer  $k.$  Hence,  $d_0 \ge 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdots 2011,$  and so we have \[a_0+2013d_0 \ge 1 + 2013(2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdots 2011) = 1 + n_0.\] This means that  $(a_0, d_0)$  is not bounded for  $n_0,$  contradicting the fact that  $(a_0, d_0)$  is valid for  $n_0.$  Therefore,  $n_0$  is bunny-unfriendly. In addition,  $n_0$  is the \textit{largest} bunny-unfriendly number whose prime factors are less than 2014; this is because \[(a_0, d_0) = (1, \, 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdots 2011)\] would be both primed and bounded (and thus valid) for any larger such integer.

The next lemma restricts the possible prime factorizations of all bunny-unfriendly integers.**Lemma 3: If  $n$  is bunny-unfriendly, then  $2013p_1p_2\cdots p_k \ge n.$**

If  $n$  is bunny-unfriendly, then the pair  $(a,d) = (1, p_1p_2\cdots p_k)$  is not valid. However, all of the elements in  $H_{a,d}$  are  $1$  mod all of the primes  $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k,$  so every element in  $H_{a,d}$  is relatively prime to  $n$ ; thus,  $(a,d)$  is primed for  $n.$  Therefore, it must be the case that  $(a,d)$  is not bounded for  $n.$  Then we must have 
	\[\begin{aligned} a+2013d &\ge n 
	1 + 2013p_1p_2\cdots p_k &\ge n  
	1 &\ge n - 2013p_1p_2 \cdots p_k \end{aligned}\]
Now notice that the right hand side of this inequality is a multiple of  $p_1p_2\cdots p_k,$  so it can never be exactly equal to  $1.$  Therefore, we can strengthen this inequality to
	\[0 \ge n - 2013p_1p_2 \cdots p_k\]
or 
	\[2013p_1p_2\cdots p_k \ge n\]
as requested.  $\square$ Because  $n$  is a multiple of  $p_1p_2\cdots p_k,$  by the above lemma, we have  $n = Fp_1p_2\cdots p_k,$  where  $F$  is an integer satisfying  $1 \ge F \ge 2013.$  Therefore, any bunny-unfriendly integer  $n$  is a product of distinct primes multiplied by the constant  $F.$  (For example, the integer  $n_0 = 2013(2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdots 2011),$  which we investigated after proving Lemma 2, is a product of distinct primes multiplied by 2013.)</details>

stem_md: Niki and Kyle play a triangle game. Niki first draws  $\triangle ABC$  with area  $1$ , and Kyle picks a point  $X$  inside  $\triangle ABC$ . Niki then draws segments  $\overline{DG}$ ,  $\overline{EH}$ , and  $\overline{FI}$ , all through  $X$ , such that  $D$  and  $E$  are on  $\overline{BC}$ ,  $F$  and  $G$  are on  $\overline{AC}$ , and  $H$  and  $I$  are on  $\overline{AB}$ . The ten points must all be distinct. Finally, let  $S$  be the sum of the areas of triangles  $DEX$ ,  $FGX$ , and  $HIX$ . Kyle earns  $S$  points, and Niki earns  $1-S$  points. If both players play optimally to maximize the amount of points they get, who will win and by how much?
solution_md:
**Lemma:** Suppose Kyle picks a point with barycentric coordinate  $(a,b,c)$ , i.e.  $X = aA + bB + cC$  where  $a + b + c = 1$ . Then the best Niki can do pickings points  $D,E,F$  is to have Kyle get only  $4(ab + ac + bc) - 1$  points. **Proof:**
Consider the quadrilaterals  $ABDG, CEHA, CFIB$ . Remark that  $[DEX] + [FGX] + [HIX] = 2[ABC] - [ABDG] - [CEHA] - [CFIB]$ . Thus it suffices to compute the areas of each of these quadrilaterals. Take an affine transformation which maps  $ABC$  to a 45-45-90 triangle with legs of side length  $1$  where  $\angle B$  is  $90$  degrees,  $A = (1,0)$  and  $C = (0,1)$  (remark that as an affine transformation preserves ratios of areas, the barycentric coordinates of  $X$  stay the same). First let's focus on  $[CEHA]$ . Putting points in the Cartesian plane we have  $X = (a,c)$ . Let  $E = (0,x)$  and one can easily compute that  $H = \left ( \frac{ax}{x-c}, 0 \right )$ . All areas written are written as a ratio with respect to [ABC], because writing all these values over 2 is a pain. We have that:

\[
[CEHA] = 1  - [EBH] = 1 - \frac{ax^2}{x-c}
\]

One can easily verify by differentiating with respect to  $x$  that all the local minima of this function lie at  $x=2c$ . Furthermore the derivative is negative when  $x > 2c$  and positive when  $x < 2c$ , so it follows at  $x=2c$  the area is a global maximum. Therefore it follows the area of  $[CEHA]$  is at most  $1 - 4ac$ . By a similar argument we can bound  $[ABDG]$  and  $[CFIB]$   by  $1 - 4ab$  and  $1 - 4bc$ . Therefore it follows the sum of the three triangle’s areas is at minimum  $2 - (3 - 4ab - 4ac - 4bc)  = 4(ab + ac + bc) - 1$  as desired (and note equality can be reached as we explicitly found where the global extrema are).  $\square$  

Now, remark that 

\[
ab + ac + bc = \frac{(a+b+c)^2 - a^2 - b^2 - c^2}{2} \le \frac{1 - \frac{1}{3}}{2} = \frac{1}{3}
\]

Thus Niki can draw triangles with minimum area sum of at most  $\frac{4}{3} - 1 = \frac{1}{3}$  for all configurations. Equality is met when  $X$  is the centroid of the triangle and Kyle gets  $\frac{1}{3}$  points which is his maximum, so it follows under optimal play that Niki wins by  $\frac{1}{3}$  points.

stem_md: Let  $ABCD$  be a quadrilateral with  $\overline{AB}\parallel\overline{CD}$ ,  $AB=16$ ,  $CD=12$ , and  $BC<AD$ . A circle with diameter  $12$  is inside of  $ABCD$  and tangent to all four sides. Find  $BC$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let the circle have center  $O$  and  $W, X, Y, Z$  be circle  $O$ 's tangency points with  $AB, BC, CD, DA$  respectively.   Notice  $\angle OWB = \angle OYC = 90$  so  $WOY$  is a straight line and the altitude of the trapezoid. Also notice \[28 = AB + CD = AW + WB + DY + YC = AZ + BX + DZ + CX = AD + BC\]
Now let  $M$  be the foot of the altitude from  $D$  to  $AB$  and  $N$  be the foot of the altitude from  $C$  to  $AB$ . Translate  $\triangle BCN$  to  $\triangle B'C'N'$  such that  $C'N'$  coincides with  $DM$ .   We know  $AB' = 16 - 12 = 4$ , and  $AD + DB' = AD + BC = 28$ . From Heron's formula, 
\[ \dfrac{4 \cdot 12}{2} = 24 = \sqrt{s(s-AB')(s-AD)(s-DB')} \]
We know that  $\dfrac{AB' + AD + DB'}{2} = \dfrac{4 + 28}{2} = 16$ . Let  $AD = x$ , so  $DB' = 28-x$ . This means \begin{eqnarray*}
24 &=& \sqrt{s(s-AB')(s-AD)(s-DB')}  &=& \sqrt{16(16 - 4)(16 - x)(16 - (28-x))}  &=& \sqrt{16 \cdot 12 \cdot (16-x)(x-12)} \end{eqnarray*}
Simplifying this gives \[ 576 = 192(16-x)(x-12) \implies 3 = (16-x)(x-12) \]
Solving the Quadratic gives  $x = 13, 15$ , or  $28-x = 15, 13$ . This means  $BC, AD$  are  $15, 13$ .   Since  $BC < AD$ , we have  $BC = \boxed{13}$ .  $\blacksquare$</details>

solution_md:
<details><summary>My solution</summary>Define the function  $f(n):=n+6\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k(n-k)$ . First, we prove by induction the identity  $f(n)=n^3$ . This holds for  $n=1$ :  $f(1)=1+0=1^3$ . Assuming  $f(n)=n^3$  for some  $n$ , it is enough to prove that  $f(n+1)=(n+1)^3$ . Indeed, 
\[f(n+1)-f(n)=\left(n+1+6\sum_{k=1}^n k(n+1-k)\right)-\left(n+6\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k(n-k)\right)=\]
\[=(n+1)-n+6\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\left[k(n+1-k)-k(n-k)\right]+6n(n+1-n)=6n+1+6\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k,\]
and it is well-known that  $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k=\frac{n(n-1)}2$ , hence
\[f(n+1)-f(n)=6n+1+6\frac{n(n-1)}2=6n+1+3n(n-1)=3n^2+3n+1,\]
or  $f(n+1)=f(n)+3n^2+3n+1=(n+1)^3$ , as needed.
Define  $A_n:=\sum_{i=1}^n (n+1-i)a_i=na_1+(n-1)a_2+\dots+a_n$ ; we know that  $A_n<0$   $\forall n\in\mathbb{Z},n>1$  because  $(a_i)$  is a spooky sequence. Moreover,  $A_1=a_1=1$ . This means that
\[S_n:=A_n+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} 6kA_{n-k}<6(n-1)A_1=6(n-1).\]
Now expand the left-hand side:
\[S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n (n+1-i)a_i+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n-k} 6k(n-k+1-i)a_i.\]
In the last double summation, a certain  $a_i$  is counted exactly for the  $k$  satisfying  $i\le n-k(<n)$ , or  $0<k\le n-i$ . Hence, we may rewrite  $S_n$  as
\[S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n (n+1-i)a_i+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n-i} 6k(n-k+1-i)a_i=\]
\[=(n+1-n)a_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} a_i\left[(n-i+1)+6\sum_{k=1}^{n-i}k((n-i+1)-k)\right]=\]

\[=a_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f(n-i+1)a_i=\]
\[=a_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(n-i+1)^3a_i=n^3a_1+(n-1)^3a_2+\dots+2^3a_{n-1}+a_n.\]
Therefore, in the case  $n=2013$ , we get
\[2013^3a_1+2012^3a_2+\dots+2^3a_{2012}+a_{2013}<6\cdot 2012=12072<12345,\]
as needed.</details>

Now, note that  $n^3=6\binom{n+2}{3}-6\binom{n+1}{2}+n$ , so \[n^3a_1+(n-1)^3a_2+...+1^3a_n=6e_n-6d_n+c_n=6(d_1+d_2+...+d_n)-6d_n+(d_n-d_{n-1})=6(d_1+d_2+...+d_{n-2})+5d_{n-1}+d_n<6(n-1)\] For  $n=2013$  the last inequality proves the result.</details>

Actually without using the second condition I got that it is less than  $6\cdot2012=12072$ .

The cleanest solution to this problem is probably "smoothing" (this does not use the 2nd condition, and still gets  $\le 12072$ ). So more explicitly, let  $S_n = na_1+(n-1)a_2+ \ldots + 2a_{n-1}+a_n$ . Actually we "weaken" the first condition to  $S_n \le 0$  for all  $n \ge 2$ . So let  $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2014}$  be a spooky subsequence that satisfies the conditions. Assume  $S_k = -j < 0$  for some  $k \ge 2$ . Let this  $k$  be the smallest. Now do the transformation  $(a_{k-1}, a_{k}, a_{k+1}) \Longrightarrow (a_{k}+j, a_{k+1}-2j, a_{k+2}+j)$ . Direct computation shows that after this transformation, 2 things hold true: 1) For  $2 \le i \le k, S_i = 0$ . 2)  $S_n \le  0$  for all  $n \ge 2$ . Also, another computation shows that the value of  $2013^3a_1+2012^3a_2+2011^3a_3+\cdots+2^3a_{2012}+a_{2013}$  increases. Therefore we can assume that all the  $S_n = 0$  (for  $n \le 2014$  or whatever). Then we get from the previous statement that  $a_1 = 1, a_2 = -2, a_3 = 1, a_i = 0$  for  $i \ge 4$ . So our max is achieved is  $2013^3-2 \cdot 2012^3+2011^3 = 12072 < 12345$ .

The nicest thing about doing this is that it HAS to work, or else the problem is false, as in by smoothing I reduce it to the optimal case, which has to hold true.
